translationRepairs: In 208 Cao Cao abolished the old Han ministerial posts, restored the chancellorship, and filled it himself, concentrating supreme executive power.
In the thirteenth year of Jian'an (208), the Han ministerial posts were abolished, the chancellorship was reinstated, and Lord Cao held it, thereby combining the highest civil authority.
The Chinese is impersonal: Han terrace offices were abolished and Lord Cao then occupied the restored chancellorship; the original wrongly makes Cao Cao the agent of the abolition.

Hidden dragons and soaring swans, talents weighed like gold against jade—think of Baili Xi, of Zichan's picks, or Chu officers serving Jin: the tools of antiquity for finding ministers were plain enough.
Hidden dragons and soaring swans, talents weighed like gold against jade—Qin Xi, Zheng Chan, and Chu talent employed by Jin: these too were fine instruments of former times, and no less manifest.
秦奚 and 鄭產 are named exemplars; 'Zichan's picks' invents a possessive, and Baili Xi is an identification not written in this sentence.
When the Three Corps followed, they swelled with crack troops like the ancient palace guard.
When the Three Corps were established, there were masses like those of Xiong Qu and Ci Fei.
The original drops 熊渠 and 佽飛, which must be restored; but 三部 here continues the Two Guards as military corps, not the civil Three Departments.
The cluster full headquarters, ritual parity with the Three Departments was Han in origin.
Opening a headquarters with ritual parity with the Three Excellencies was a Han office.
The original is ungrammatical and does not render the office 開府儀同三司; the replacement states the Han office accurately.
Otherwise old rules held through three reigns until collapse.
The rest followed the old regulations through the three reigns of Wu, Hui, and Xiaohuai.
The Chinese names Wu, Hui, and Xiaohuai and does not mention collapse; the original invents that ending and drops the reign names.
In 216 Xiahou Dun commanded twenty-six armies after the Wu campaign—a milestone.
In 216, returning from the campaign against Sun Quan, Xiahou Dun supervised twenty-six armies; this is an instance.
The campaign is against 孫權 and 是也 marks an example, not a milestone; both points are restored.
227 CE Sima Yi took the supreme commander title for the Shu expedition.
In the autumn of Emperor Ming of Wei's fourth Taihe year, Prince Xuan campaigned against Shu and added the title supreme commander.
The original fuses 227 CE onto Sima Yi and omits Emperor Ming of Wei, autumn, and the source title 宣帝.
Under Zhang of Later Han, Grand Tutor Zhao Xi and Minister of War Mou Rong both recorded Secretariat affairs.
Under Emperor Zhang of Later Han, Grand Tutor Zhao Xi and Minister of War Mou Rong both recorded Secretariat affairs.
漢章帝 is Emperor Zhang; bare 'Zhang' reads as a personal name rather than the Later Han emperor.

In the fourth year of Jiushi under Chengdi the Zhongshu eunuchs were abolished and five Masters of Writing were again appointed—one serving as vice director and four forming four bureaus jointly handling archives, secret records, and memorials, each with its charge.

In the fourth year of Jianshi under Chengdi the Zhongshu eunuchs were abolished and five Masters of Writing were again appointed—one serving as vice director and four forming four bureaus jointly handling archives, secret records, and memorials, each with its charge.
建始 romanizes as Jianshi; Jiushi is a different invented era name.
When Wu founded the Secretariat in 29 BCE he attached four assistant commissioners.
When Emperor Wu of Han established the Secretariat in the fourth year of Jianshi, four assistants were immediately placed.
The source pairs 漢武帝 with 建始四年; converting that pairing to 29 BCE and clipping the emperor to 'Wu' hides the wording the chapter actually uses.

chief clerk, merit clerk, household commander, recorder, armor office, gentlemen-thieves office, camp army, malfeasance clerk, household-area commander, merit clerk assistants, gate clerks, household clerks—one each.

registrar, merit clerk, household commander, recorder, armor-and-gentlemen-thieves offices, camp-army and malfeasance clerks, household-area commander, merit-clerk assistants and gate clerks, household clerks—one each.
主簿 is the registrar; calling it a second chief clerk collides with 長史 in the preceding sentence.
234 CE added Capital Officials and Cavalry bureaus for twenty-five lines.
In the second year of Qinglong, Minister Chen Jiao memorialized to add Capital Officials and Cavalry, making twenty-five gentlemen in all.
The original drops 青龍二年 and the memorialist 陳矯, leaving only a Western year and bureau names.
Attendants traced to Feng Hou; Zhou called similar posts permanent stewards; Qin revived the title and Han kept it.

Palace attendants are traced to Feng Hou under the Yellow Emperor; under Zhou the duty matched the permanent steward; Qin borrowed the ancient name to establish palace attendants, and Han continued it.
風後 is palace attendant under 黃帝; the original omits the Yellow Emperor.
Wei fused freelance riders with standing attendants as feather-light counselors—fur pouch on the right, mounted escort—and Jin kept the mold.

At the start of Huangchu, Emperor Wen of Wei restored unattached cavalry and merged them with palace standing attendants to offer counsel without managing affairs; marten-fur bags were tucked on the right as they rode in loose escort—unchanged through Jin.
The merger is dated 魏文帝黃初初 and includes 同掌規諫，不典事; the original flattens this to generic 'Wei'.
296 CE briefly saw the eunuch Dong Meng as standing attendant—then the experiment ended.
In Yuankang, Emperor Hui first made the eunuch Dong Meng a palace standing attendant; afterward the practice stopped.
The Chinese names 元康中 and 惠帝; a lone 296 CE year erases both the era and the appointing emperor.
Wu invented supernumerary deputies; 318 CE Yuan rotated two with regular deputies—'general-access' deputies—and later raised them to four.

Originally Emperor Wu established supernumerary elite cavalry deputy gentlemen; in the first year of Taixing, Emperor Yuan made two men rotate jointly with the elite cavalry deputy gentlemen—hence general-access elite cavalry deputy gentlemen—later increased to four.
Bare 'Wu' and '318 CE Yuan' obscure 武帝 and 元帝 and drop 太興元年.
Later Han cashiered the Three Dukes and packed the audience rolls with kin and nobles.
In Eastern Han, many of the Three Dukes, imperial in-laws, imperial clansmen, and nobles held court-attending status.
三公、外戚、宗室、諸侯 are listed together as groups who often held 奉朝請; the original treats 罷 as cashiering the Three Dukes alone.
Wudi named Miao Zheng Zhongshu compiler.
Wudi named Miao Zheng as Zhongshu compiler.
Without as, 'Miao Zheng Zhongshu compiler' can be read as a fused personal name rather than appointee plus office.
364 CE folded the Chamberlain for Attendants into the Minister of Education.
光祿勳 is the Chamberlain for Attendants, not the Coachman (太僕); 司徒 is the Minister of Education.
In the second year of Xing'ning under Emperor Ai the Imperial Coachman was abolished and merged into the Minister of Education.
In the second year of Xing'ning under Emperor Ai the Chamberlain for Attendants was abolished and merged into the Minister of Education.
The abolished office is 光祿勳, not the Imperial Coachman.
373 CE revived the Chamberlain for Attendants.
復置 resumes the 光祿勳 just named, not the Coachman.
Han titled empress-dowager suites above homonymous ministers; without a dowager the seats stayed empty.

The Three Ministers of the Empress Dowager—Commandant of the Guards, Privy Treasurer, and Minister Coachman—were established in Han; their titles followed the empress dowager's palace, ranking above ministers of the same name, and stayed vacant when there was no empress dowager.
The sentence names the three Han offices 衛尉、少府、太僕, their palace-based titles, and vacancy without a dowager; 'suites' erases all of that.
Han kept the pattern; in 7 BCE the censor-in-chief became Grand Minister of Works with a chief clerk, but the assistant director stayed unchanged.

Han followed this; in the first year of Suihe under Emperor Cheng (7 BCE) the Censor-in-Chief was renamed Grand Minister of Works and a chief clerk was established, while the assistant director's duties remained as before.
The renaming is 成帝綏和元年; a Western year alone omits the emperor and era name.

Under Jin, nine posts were established at the same grade as document clerks, but they covered thirteen desks: Personnel, Merit Ranking, Duty Affairs, Seals, Inner Area Command, Outer Area Command, Matchmaking, Tallies, Water, Inner Rampart, Camp Army, Law, and Arithmetic.

Under Jin, nine posts were established at the same grade as the law-editing attendant censors, but they covered thirteen desks: Personnel, Merit Ranking, Duty Affairs, Seals, Inner Area Command, Outer Area Command, Matchmaking, Tallies, Water, Inner Rampart, Camp Army, Law, and Arithmetic.
品同治書 matches the grade of the law-editing attendant censors (治書侍御史), not generic document clerks.
As Prince of Jin he ran forces for the future emperor.
When the emperor was Prince of Jin, he entrusted him to manage military affairs.
帝為晉王 continues 文帝 as Prince of Jin commissioning Chen Xie; the original invents a separate future emperor as beneficiary.
After Shu's fall Chen Xie absorbed Zhuge Liang's formations and dual-camp signals—Wudi made him hall corps gentleman then general.

After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and the hidden methods of maneuver and ambush, as well as the first-and-second camp banner system; Xie practiced them all to mastery and was therefore made palace hall gentleman commanding troops, later promoted general.
The subject of 令勰 remains the same 帝 (Wen as Prince of Jin); naming Wudi as appointer is not in this sentence, and 暗練 is practiced mastery.

After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and maneuver secrets of troops and ambush, as well as the first-second camp banner systems—Xie mastered them all in darkness; therefore Xie was made palace hall gentleman commanding troops as gentleman-of-the-palace, later promoted general.

After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and methods of troop maneuvers and ambush, as well as the first-and-second camp banner system; Xie practiced them all to fluency; therefore Xie was made palace hall gentleman commanding troops, later promoted general.
暗練 is practiced fluency, not 'in darkness', and 中郎將 must not be doubled; the proposal's 'gentleman-of-the-household' and 'A/B' wording are still awkward.
Under Jin, Colonel Directors, Colonel Protectors, Left and Right Guards, Valiant Cavalry, and Mobile Corps formed the Six Armies.
Under Jin, the Army Commander, Army Protector, Left and Right Guards, Valiant Cavalry, and Mobile Corps formed the Six Armies.
領、護 in this chapter are the Army Commander and Army Protector, not Colonel Directors and Protectors.
Nightfall stranded the train past water-clock closing time—the royal coach shell stuck open until Wudi told Chen Xie to seal it.

The carriage turned back only when dusk pressed close; the clepsydra had run out, and the armored coach-box should have been closed; they halted the imperial carriage and long could not close it, so an edict ordered Xie to close it.
This sentence has 詔勰, an edict, without naming Wudi as an oral speaker; the original invents that telling.
Wudi's heir's palace began with a central guard rate.
The Left and Right Guard Rates: when Wudi built the Eastern Palace he established guard rates, first called the Central Guard Rate.
The lemma is 左右衛率 and 東宮 was built by Emperor Wu and first called 中衛率; the proposal still drops the left-and-right heading, while 'heir's palace' is only a gloss.

In the third year of Xianning Guards General Yang Yao and Palace Secretariat supervisor Xun Xu, fearing later troubles for Emperor Hui, cited former Minister of Works Pei Xiu's feudal plan and told Emperor Wu: "In antiquity establishing nobility was to screen and guard the royal house.

In the third year of Xianning, Guards General Yang Yao and Palace Secretariat supervisor Xun Xu, because Prince You of Qi enjoyed timely prestige and they feared later troubles for Emperor Hui, cited former Minister of Works Pei Xiu's five-grade feudal intent and calmly presented contemporary policy to Emperor Wu, saying: "In antiquity establishing nobility was to screen and guard the royal house.
The original omits 齊王攸有時望, the five-grade feudal intent, and 從容共陳時宜.
Only Lu gained extra households; Shen and Yang Hu were bumped posthumously.

Only the Lu ducal fief had its households specially increased; former Minister of Works Duke of Boling Wang Shen was advanced to commandery duke, and Marquis of Juping Yang Hu to commandery marquis of Nancheng.
Clipped 'Shen' hides 王沈, and the original drops the specific titles; 追進封故司空 applies to Wang Shen, not a vague joint bump.
Enforcement sent peers weeping from Luoyang.
Once implemented, those whose fiefs had been augmented were sent to their domains as originally memorialized, yet the dukes clung to the capital and departed weeping.
The Chinese has 京師, not Luoyang, and specifies that the augmented transfers went to their fiefs as originally memorialized.
